C0.quote: We consider electoral control by deleting voters.
C0.note: Strategic/computational aspects of plurality voting: voter-deletion control under LDP polls.

C1.quote: we establish two integer linear programs to give a general upper and lower bound
C1.note: Main results are ILP/LP-based computation of manipulation cost and closed-form APoLDP. Control is the attack model (SB). Numeric experiments on synthetic data and Sushi-derived types (SI).

C2.1.value: true type / reported type (of preference); votes
C2.1.quote: we define the type of his/her preference as the candidate he/she votes for

C2.2.quote: We focus on the plurality rule (e.g., each voter votes for exactly one candidate)
C2.2.note: Plurality single-candidate votes, modelled as types in [1,m]; none of the listed formats fits.

C2.3.quote: the type of true preference of each voter (we refer to it as true type)
C2.3.note: True preference/type is held; reported type is generated by the LDP mechanism.

C2.4.quote: Voters will vote according to their true types in the election.
C2.4.note: True type and reported type have separate notation and the reported one differs stochastically. Votes equal the true type in the election; the poll report differs.

C3.1.quote: Voters will still vote according to their true preference in the election
C3.1.note: Voters are not strategic; the LDP report deviates from the true type through a random mechanism, not voter choice. The only strategic agent is the attacker.

C3.2.quote: Voters will still vote according to their true preference in the election
C3.2.note: Stated for the election votes. The poll reports are intentionally randomized.

C3.3.quote: the mechanisms are only used in pre-election polls
C3.3.note: No incentive argument; it is a modelling setup stated by the authors. PROC is the closest fit.

C4.1.note: No voter utility or welfare notion is used.

C5.1.note: The evaluation criterion is the attacker's manipulation cost, not voter welfare.

VOT.quote_behav: Voters will still vote according to their true preference in the election
VOT.note: Voters run the LDP mechanism and vote truthfully.

BRI.quote_behav: There is an attacker who tries to make a designated candidate win
BRI.quote_info: he/she only knows the reported preference of voters instead of their true preference
BRI.note: The attacker is an external controller deleting voters, so BRI is the closest type (alternatively ORG). It knows reported types and λ, not the true types.

DES.note: The choice of ε is only guidance, not modelled.

C7.1.quote: There is an attacker who tries to make a designated candidate win
C7.1.note: BRI (attacker) is STRAT while VOT is NONSTRAT.

C7.2.note: The paper gives no reason for modelling voters as non-strategic.

C8.1.quote: the minimal number of voters the attacker should delete as the manipulation cost
C8.1.note: Control by deletion treated as an optimisation problem.

claims.quote: provide general guidance towards the application of LDP mechanisms
show that they can generally enhance the resilience of a voting system
gives general guidance towards the choice of the privacy parameter

C9.1.note: Claims about real institutions and which ε to use.

C9.2.quote: we can use a two-round implementation of LDP in voting to estimate λ
C9.2.note: The claims need an assumption about the attacker's knowledge of λ, which is stated and discussed. Also needed: voters have no incentive to misreport or vote strategically, which is not argued, and the applicability of the plurality-only results to real elections.
